sentences.text: Huabeisaurus was a sauropod dinosaur that lived in northern China during the Late Cretaceous.
This animal measured 20 meters in total length and stood 5 meters high, making it large compared to most dinosaurs but only midsized by sauropod standards.
Two well-preserved teeth with wrinkled enamel were recovered from the holotype, one found in the quarry and a second discovered during field sample preparation at Shijiazhuang University.
Twelve chevrons are currently preserved in the holotype, covering nearly the entire length of the caudal vertebral series.
The absence of sutures on the vertebrae suggests the specimen was nearing sexual maturity, while open sutures on the scapula and ilium suggest it had not reached full maturity.
The species Huabeisaurus allocotus was first described by Pang Qiqing and Cheng Zhengwu in the year 2000.
Numerous remains, including teeth, partial limbs, and vertebrae, were found in the 1990s.
Fossils were discovered at Kangdailiang and Houyu in Zhaojiagou Town, Tianzhen County, Shanxi province, China.
The holotype was found in the upper member of the Huiquanpu Formation, dated to the Late Cretaceous using ostracods, charophytes, and fission-track dating.
The holotype specimen originally contained 32 caudal vertebrae before some were lost during fossilization or collection.

D'Emic et al. (2013) identified several unique features of Huabeisaurus, including divided vertebral laminae, specific caudal rib patterns, a coracoid with a tubercle, and a high tibia-to-femur ratio.
The geological horizon containing an isolated Huabeisaurus humerus also yielded hadrosaurid specimens and indeterminate ankylosaurid material.
The type locality of Huabeisaurus has also produced the ankylosaur Tianzhenosaurus and theropod material referred to cf. Szechuanosaurus campi.
The discoverers erected the family Huabeisauridae for the genus to include Huabeisaurus and the closely related Tangvayosaurus, though this name is not widely used by paleontologists.
Huabeisaurus is classified within the family Saltasauridae and belongs to the parent group Euhelopodidae.
Huabeisaurus belongs to the parent group Euhelopodidae.

A set of 12 characters identified by D'Emic et al. in 2013 differentiate Huabeisaurus from other sauropods, including divided presacral vertebral laminae, divided prezygodiapophyseal laminae in posterior cervical vertebrae, divided anterior spinodiapophyseal laminae in anterior dorsal vertebrae, a larger postzygapophyseal spinodiapophyseal fossa than the postzygapophyseal centrodiapophyseal fossa in anterior and middle caudal vertebrae, small caudal ribs disappearing around the eighth caudal vertebra, posterior expansion of the anterior and middle caudal vertebral centra by one-third, two longitudinal crests on the lateral faces of the mid-caudal vertebral centra, a coracoid with a tubercle near the anterodorsal edge of the lateral face, a distal radius approximately twice as wide transversely as the mid-shaft, a tubercle on the ischial plate projecting from the posterior margin, relative fossae development in caudal neural arches, and a high tibia-to-femur ratio.
The holotype of Huabeisaurus was found in the upper member of the Huiquanpu Formation, dated to the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian to Campanian) using ostracods, charophytes, and fission-track dating.
It remains uncertain how long the endemism of East Asian sauropods, including Huabeisaurus, lasted.
Pang and Cheng tentatively suggested that Titanosaurus falloti belongs to Huabeisaurus, but this is disputed because the femur lacks uniquely shared features.
